concepts_used: Article 368: Scope, Procedure, and Limitations

solution.concept_anchor: State ratification threshold under Article 368
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because the word 'all' sounds constitutionally authoritative, and students often reason that state sovereignty demands unanimous consent for federal changes.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): there is no time limit prescribed under Article 368 for state ratification — the Constitution is silent on this.
Eliminate option (b): ratification by all states is not required; Article 368 requires only a majority of state legislatures, not unanimity.
Eliminate option (d): 'all states' is an overstatement; the correct threshold is more than half (50%) of the total states.
Confirm option (c): Article 368 specifies ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the states, with no time limit attached.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently conflate the state ratification requirement with unanimity, reasoning by analogy with federal systems like the USA where supermajority of states is required. The Indian Constitution requires ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the states — a simple numerical majority of states, not all of them. Additionally, the Constitution prescribes no time limit within which states must ratify, a detail that trips candidates who assume Parliament can set a deadline.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 establishes a three-tier amendment procedure. The most stringent tier requires a special majority in Parliament AND ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the total states. This applies to provisions touching federalism — such as election of the President, extent of executive power of Union and States, and representation in Rajya Sabha.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No time limit for ratification exists under Article 368. States can ratify at any time without constitutional compulsion of a deadline.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'All states' is never required. The threshold is at least half of all states.
• Option (c) — Correct: More than half of states must ratify, and no time limit is prescribed — this is the precise constitutional requirement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Same error as (b); universality is not the standard.

Value Addition:
• Ratification must come from state legislatures, not state governments or governors.
• The President cannot withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill — made mandatory by the 24th Amendment.
• Only about 8–10 categories of provisions require state ratification.

solution.concept_anchor: First Amendment 1951 — Ninth Schedule genesis

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserted the Ninth Schedule to place certain laws beyond challenge on grounds of Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment precisely to shield land reform legislation from being struck down under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 was enacted to override the Supreme Court's ruling in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras.
statement_analysis.reason: The First Amendment responded to the judgment in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan. Gopalan dealt with preventive detention, not property rights or educational reservations.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment expanded the grounds on which the State could impose reasonable restrictions on the right to free speech under Article 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The Amendment inserted 'reasonable restrictions' language in Articles 19(2) and 19(4), broadening the grounds — including public order and relations with foreign states — on which free speech could be curtailed.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who recall the Ninth Schedule correctly may also conflate the Champakam Dorairajan case with A.K. Gopalan, both of which were landmark early 1950s Supreme Court decisions.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The Ninth Schedule was indeed added by the First Amendment to protect land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges — this is accurate.
Eliminate Statement 2 as incorrect: The relevant Supreme Court case was Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan — entity-swap trap; any option pairing Statement 2 as correct must be eliminated.
Confirm Statement 3: Expanded restrictions on Article 19 rights were a direct feature of the First Amendment — correct.
The only option with Statements 1 and 3 correct and Statement 2 incorrect is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) is a famous early Supreme Court case about personal liberty under Article 21, not about property rights or educational reservations. The First Amendment was Parliament's direct response to State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, which invalidated communal reservation in educational institutions. A candidate who has memorised both landmark cases but not their specific triggers will easily confuse them here.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) was Parliament's earliest assertion of its authority over judicial interpretations of Fundamental Rights. It responded directly to Champakam Dorairajan, where the Supreme Court struck down caste-based reservation in admissions to state colleges.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Ninth Schedule was created by this amendment to insulate land reform laws from judicial review under Part III.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The triggering case was Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan. Gopalan concerned preventive detention and Article 21.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Articles 19(2) and 19(4) were amended to add broader grounds for restricting free speech, including public order and incitement to offences.

Value Addition:
• The First Amendment is historically significant as the first instance of Parliament overriding a Supreme Court judgment through a constitutional amendment.
• The Ninth Schedule originally contained only 13 laws; it grew to 284 laws over decades.
• The First Amendment is also the genesis of the Parliament–Judiciary conflict over constitutional supremacy.

solution.concept_anchor: 7th Amendment 1956 — state reorganization and Rajya Sabha

statement_analysis.statement: The Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 abolished the four-tier classification of Indian states and replaced it with a two-category framework of States and Union Territories.
statement_analysis.reason: The Seventh Amendment eliminated the Parts A, B, C, and D classification and introduced the simpler States and Union Territories distinction, in line with the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: The Seventh Amendment did not require state ratification because it only reorganized state territories and did not affect the federal character of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Seventh Amendment revised Schedule 4 (Rajya Sabha seat allocation), which affects representation of states in the Council of States — a provision requiring state ratification under Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: The Seventh Amendment prohibited the establishment of a common High Court for more than one state, requiring each state to maintain its own High Court.
statement_analysis.reason: The opposite is true — Article 231 was inserted by the Seventh Amendment to specifically enable Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or a state and a Union Territory.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who know Statement 2 is wrong may not verify Statement 3, assuming it is correct since common High Courts appear to be a logical post-reorganisation feature.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The four-tier to two-category change is historically accurate — Statement 1 is correct, so it cannot be the answer to 'NOT correct'.
Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that no state ratification was needed is false — Rajya Sabha representation changes trigger the ratification requirement.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 231 explicitly allows common High Courts — so the claim that they were prohibited is false.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct; option (a) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The ratification requirement is the core trap here. Many students assume that mere territorial reorganization does not affect the federal character enough to trigger state ratification. However, because Schedule 4 (Rajya Sabha seats) was revised, the amendment crossed the threshold requiring state concurrence. Statement 3 is a reversal trap — students who know common High Courts exist may incorrectly credit Statement 3 as true without recalling that the Seventh Amendment specifically enabled, not prohibited, them.
solution.final_explanation:
The Seventh Amendment (1956) was a sweeping structural change following the States Reorganisation Act and the Dar Commission recommendations. It fundamentally altered India's federal architecture.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Parts A/B/C/D system was scrapped; the modern States and Union Territories framework was introduced.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Because Schedule 4 (Rajya Sabha allocation) was revised, state ratification under Article 368 was required — and obtained.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: Article 231 was inserted precisely to permit common High Courts for two or more states, the opposite of what the statement claims.

Value Addition:
• Currently, common High Courts exist for Punjab and Haryana (High Court at Chandigarh).
• The Seventh Amendment also made it possible to appoint a judge to act in another High Court — Article 224A.
• The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali Commission) recommended linguistic reorganisation of states, which the Seventh Amendment gave constitutional effect to.

concepts_used: 24th Amendment Act, 1971: Parliament's Absolute Power to Amend Fundamental Rights
Doctrine of Implied Limitations and the Golak Nath–Kesavananda–Minerva Mills Trilogy

solution.concept_anchor: 24th Amendment 1971 — overruling Golak Nath

statement_analysis.statement: The 24th Amendment overruled Golak Nath v. State of Punjab by amending Article 13 to clarify that constitutional amendments are not 'law' within the meaning of that Article.
statement_analysis.reason: The 24th Amendment explicitly added a new clause to Article 13 stating that nothing in Article 13 applies to an amendment made under Article 368, directly reversing Golak Nath's holding.

statement_analysis.statement: The 24th Amendment made Presidential assent to constitutional amendment bills discretionary, leaving the President free to withhold consent.
statement_analysis.reason: The 24th Amendment made Presidential assent mandatory — it removed any discretion the President might have had; the President is obligated to give assent.

statement_analysis.statement: The 24th Amendment was entirely upheld by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
statement_analysis.reason: The 24th Amendment was only partially upheld — the court accepted Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights but subjected it to the Basic Structure limitation, meaning the amendment was not given unconditional validity.

statement_analysis.statement: The 24th Amendment affirmed Parliament's power to amend any provision of the Constitution, including provisions relating to Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: This was the central purpose of the 24th Amendment — to assert that Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 extends to Fundamental Rights, reversing Golak Nath's restrictive interpretation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is the strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 4 as correct and Statement 2 as incorrect may mistakenly accept Statement 3 as correct, recalling only that Kesavananda 'upheld' some aspects of the 24th Amendment.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is accurate — the clause added to Article 13 is a documented feature of the 24th Amendment; mark correct.
Statement 2 is reversed — the 24th Amendment made Presidential assent mandatory, not discretionary; mark incorrect.
Statement 3 overstates — Kesavananda partially upheld the 24th Amendment but imposed the Basic Structure limitation; 'entirely upheld' is false; mark incorrect.
Statement 4 is the core purpose of the amendment — Parliament can amend any part including FR; mark correct. Only two statements (1 and 4) are correct — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the critical trap. Students with partial knowledge recall that the 24th Amendment was 'validated' in Kesavananda Bharati and assume this means full validation. In reality, the court imposed the Basic Structure doctrine as a limit — so Parliament's amending power was confirmed but qualified. Saying the amendment was 'entirely upheld' is therefore incorrect. This distinction between partial and full judicial validation is a recurring UPSC testing zone.
solution.final_explanation:
The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's direct legislative reply to the Supreme Court's Golak Nath judgment (1967), which had held that Fundamental Rights could not be amended at all. Parliament responded by asserting its constituent power through amendments to both Articles 13 and 368.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 13 was amended to exclude constitutional amendments from the definition of 'law', neutralising Golak Nath.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Presidential assent was made mandatory, not discretionary — a significant shift in executive-legislative dynamics.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) only partially upheld the 24th Amendment — it accepted Parliament's power to amend FR but imposed the Basic Structure limitation, which was not unconditional validation.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Affirming parliamentary power over FR was the central object of the amendment.

Value Addition:
• Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — the answer is 'Only two'.
• The 24th Amendment is part of the Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda trilogy.
• Mandatory Presidential assent to amendment bills remains operative today.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

4. It affirmed Parliament's power to amend any provision of the Constitution, including provisions relating to Fundamental Rights.

(b) Only two
(c) Only three

solution.concept_anchor: Basic Structure — cases and elements
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may correctly pair free and fair elections with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain but then misremember that Kesavananda itself mentioned the separation of powers explicitly.
elimination_logic: Free and fair elections as a Basic Structure element was identified in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), not Kesavananda — this eliminates options where A is matched to 1.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is correctly matched with supremacy of the Constitution and republican democratic form — List II item 2 is the correct match for A.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) dealt with the Tenth Schedule and Speaker's authority, not Basic Structure elements per se — match D to 4.
Minerva Mills (1980) added harmony between FR and DPSPs — match C to 3. Confirm: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in attributing Basic Structure elements to the wrong case. 'Free and fair elections' is often remembered as a Kesavananda contribution because students associate all Basic Structure articulation with that landmark. However, Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) was the case that specifically added free and fair elections to the Basic Structure. Kesavananda focused on the foundational elements: supremacy of Constitution, democratic republican form, and secular character.
solution.final_explanation:
The Basic Structure doctrine evolved through multiple Supreme Court judgments, with each case adding new elements or reinforcing existing ones. Matching each element to its correct originating case tests precision of knowledge.

• A (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973): The foundational case identified supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, and federalism — matched to List II item 2.
• B (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975): Free and fair elections was identified as a Basic Structure element in this case arising from the Allahabad HC judgment on Indira Gandhi's election — matched to List II item 1.
• C (Minerva Mills, 1980): Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs was declared a Basic Structure element, and limited amending power was reinforced — matched to List II item 3.
• D (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992): The Speaker's authority under the Tenth Schedule was upheld but subjected to judicial review — matched to item 4.

Value Addition:
• The Basic Structure doctrine has no exhaustive codified list in the Constitution — it is entirely judge-made.
• Each major amendment from 1971–1985 was a parliamentary attempt to push back against judicial expansion of Basic Structure.
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) added federalism as an independently enforceable Basic Structure element.

concepts_used: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: The 'Mini Constitution' and Its Sweeping Changes
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Limits on Parliament's Amending Power

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment Clauses 4&5 struck down in Minerva Mills
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are factually true, and students may rush to conclude that R explains A without checking whether the causal direction is accurate.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, were struck down by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) as unconstitutional.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. The Basic Structure doctrine was established in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and holds that Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's basic features.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Partially but not precisely. The reason the clauses were struck down was specifically because Parliament cannot confer unlimited amending power on itself — i.e., the limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure element. R states the general doctrine but not the precise mechanism: the self-conferral of unlimited power was the specific violation. R is a broader true statement that does not capture the exact causal link — R is a correct background fact but not the correct explanation of A.
Since both A and R are correct but R does not precisely explain A — the answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the fact that both A and R are true, which leads most students to option (a). The trap is that R states the general Basic Structure principle, which sounds like it explains everything. However, the precise reason Clauses 4 and 5 were struck down is a specific corollary: that Parliament cannot confer unlimited amending power upon itself, which would make the limited amending power (itself a Basic Structure element) meaningless. R captures the general doctrine, not the specific operative reason — making it a correct but non-explanatory statement.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills (1980) is one of the most consequential post-Emergency Supreme Court judgments. The 42nd Amendment had inserted Clauses 4 and 5 into Article 368, effectively immunising all constitutional amendments from judicial review and conferring unlimited amending power on Parliament.

Assertion analysis: Clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368 were indeed struck down in Minerva Mills — Assertion is correct.

Reason analysis: The Basic Structure doctrine, established in Kesavananda Bharati, limits Parliament's constituent power — Reason is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R is a correct background principle but does not precisely explain why those specific clauses were struck down. The court held that conferring unlimited amending power on Parliament itself violates Basic Structure because 'limited amending power' is a Basic Structure element. R is too general to serve as the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills also struck down the expanded Article 31C that gave all DPSPs primacy over Fundamental Rights.
• The original Article 31C (protecting only Articles 39(b) and (c)) survived Minerva Mills.
• The judgment reinforced that the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

Reason (R): The Basic Structure doctrine established in Kesavananda Bharati holds that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is not absolute and cannot be used to destroy the Constitution's essential features.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment 1978 — sequence of key changes
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students may correctly sequence the 42nd and 44th Amendments but confuse whether the deletion of the Right to Property preceded or followed the Emergency provisions changes.
elimination_logic: The 42nd Amendment (1976) preceded all the changes listed — it extended Lok Sabha terms to 6 years and was an Emergency-era amendment.
The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the 5-year term, deleted the Right to Property from FR, and strengthened Emergency safeguards — all in the same amendment.
The Right to Education (Article 21A) was inserted only by the 86th Amendment (2002) — far later than any of the above changes.
The correct sequence is: 42nd Amendment extended terms → 44th Amendment restored terms and deleted Right to Property → 86th Amendment added Right to Education. This matches option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap operates at two levels. First, students may confuse whether the deletion of the Right to Property was a 44th Amendment feature or earlier. Second, the question tests whether students know that Article 21A (Right to Education) came only in 2002 — a candidate who blurs the 44th and 86th Amendments might incorrectly place RTE earlier in the sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd–44th Amendment sequence is a critical arc in India's constitutional history, covering the Emergency period and its aftermath. The 44th Amendment (1978) specifically targeted the excesses of the Emergency era.

Correct sequence:
1. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended the terms of Lok Sabha and state assemblies from 5 to 6 years during the Emergency.
2. The 44th Amendment (1978) restored the original 5-year terms, deleted the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights (moved to Article 300A), and added safeguards against Emergency misuse — all in the same amendment.
3. The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, making the Right to Education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a): Places restoration of terms before deletion of property right — both occurred in the same amendment (44th), making internal sequencing irrelevant and the option misleading.
• Option (c): Places RTE before property deletion — reverses the correct chronological order.
• Option (d): Reverses the 42nd and 44th Amendments entirely.

Value Addition:
• Article 300A (legal right to property) remains enforceable but is not a Fundamental Right.
• Under the 44th Amendment, the President must act on written advice of the Cabinet before declaring Emergency.
• The Lok Sabha can revoke an Emergency by simple majority under the 44th Amendment framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule — Speaker's authority and judicial review
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the President does play a role in constitutional matters, and students may confuse referral to the President with the Speaker's adjudicatory role under the Tenth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan held that Speaker's orders under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review — they are not final and unchallengeable.
Eliminate option (b): Defection cases are decided by the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) — not referred to the President for adjudication.
Eliminate option (c): The Election Commission has no jurisdiction over defection matters — its role is in elections, not post-election disqualification for defection.
Confirm option (d): The Speaker is the adjudicating authority; the order can be challenged in the High Court or Supreme Court after the Speaker decides — not before.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to test whether students know that judicial review of Speaker's orders is available but only after the order is made, not as a prior check. Students who recall that 'Speaker's decision is final' from a shallow reading of the Tenth Schedule will incorrectly choose option (a). Kihoto Hollohan specifically clarified that while the Speaker has primacy, courts retain the power of judicial review of the final order.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985) provides for disqualification of legislators on grounds of defection. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (or Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) is designated as the sole adjudicating authority for defection petitions.

Applicable principle: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but held that the Speaker's orders are subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice — and only after the order is passed.

Scenario analysis: Rajan's petition must be submitted to the Speaker, who will adjudicate it. If dissatisfied, Rajan can challenge the Speaker's final order in the High Court or Supreme Court.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Speaker's orders are reviewable — they are not absolutely final.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The President is not the adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Election Commission handles election-related matters, not defection disqualifications.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Speaker adjudicates; courts can review the order after it is passed.

Value Addition:
• The 91st Amendment (2003) raised the merger threshold from 1/3rd to 2/3rd of party members.
• Defection disqualification proceedings do not bar future election candidacy.
• Para 2 of the Tenth Schedule covers voluntary giving up of party membership and voting against party whip.

solution.concept_anchor: 61st Amendment — voting age vs candidacy age

statement_analysis.statement: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 amended Article 326 to lower the minimum age for voting in elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies from 21 to 18 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 326 was amended by the 61st Amendment to reduce the voting age from 21 to 18 years for elections to both the House of the People and legislative assemblies of states.

statement_analysis.statement: As a consequence of the 61st Amendment, the minimum age for contesting elections to the Lok Sabha was also lowered to 18 years.
statement_analysis.reason: The 61st Amendment changed only the voting age (franchise), not the age of candidacy. The minimum age to contest Lok Sabha or state assembly elections remains 25 years, and for Rajya Sabha or state legislative councils, it remains 30 years.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 may assume that lowering the voting age logically implies a corresponding lowering of the candidacy age, making 'both correct' seem reasonable.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is verifiable and correct — Article 326 was amended by the 61st Amendment to reduce the voting age to 18.

Statement 2 conflates voting age (franchise) with candidacy age — these are governed by different provisions. Candidacy age for Lok Sabha is 25 years under Article 84, unchanged by the 61st Amendment.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic conflation trap — voting age and candidacy age are distinct constitutional provisions. Voting eligibility is under Article 326; candidacy requirements are under Articles 84 (Parliament) and 173 (State Legislatures). The 61st Amendment touched only Article 326. A student who merges these two concepts will incorrectly believe both were changed, selecting option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The 61st Amendment (1988) was enacted to enfranchise India's large youth population by reducing the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 326 was specifically amended; the 18-year voting age applies to both Lok Sabha and state assembly elections.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Candidacy age was not affected. Article 84 requires a candidate to be at least 25 years for Lok Sabha, and Article 173 requires the same for state assemblies. These remain unchanged.

Value Addition:
• The voting age for Rajya Sabha elections (indirect, through MLAs) is also 18 now since MLAs themselves were elected at 18+.
• Minimum age of candidacy: Lok Sabha/Vidhan Sabha = 25 years; Rajya Sabha/Vidhan Parishad = 30 years.
• This amendment required only a special majority — it does not fall under the state ratification category despite affecting elections.

solution.concept_anchor: 73rd Amendment — mandatory vs discretionary provisions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because devolution of powers to panchayats sounds like it should be mandatory — students often assume the Centre would compel states to devolve functions.
elimination_logic: Reservation of seats for SCs, STs, and women in panchayats is mandatory — states have no discretion; eliminate (a) as the odd one out.
Constitution of State Election Commissions for superintendence of panchayat elections is a mandatory requirement — eliminate (d) as the odd one out.
Direct elections to all seats in panchayats at all three tiers is mandatory — eliminate (b) as the odd one out.

Devolution of powers and functions from the Eleventh Schedule to panchayats is explicitly discretionary — states 'may' devolve; this is the only discretionary provision, making it the odd one out. Answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The mandatory vs. discretionary distinction is a classic UPSC testing zone for the 73rd Amendment. Students tend to assume that all major provisions are mandatory since the amendment has constitutional status. However, the devolution of functions from the Eleventh Schedule is a 'may' provision — the Constitution leaves it to state legislatures to decide which functions to transfer. In contrast, reservation, direct elections, and State Election Commissions are compulsory obligations on states.
solution.final_explanation:
The 73rd Amendment (1992) creates a two-tier framework: mandatory provisions that states must implement, and discretionary provisions that states may or may not adopt.

• Option (a) — Mandatory: Reservation for SCs, STs, and women (not less than one-third) in panchayat seats is compulsory under Article 243D.
• Option (b) — Mandatory: Direct elections to all panchayat seats at all three tiers (village, intermediate, district) are obligatory under Article 243C.
• Option (c) — Discretionary and the ODD ONE OUT: Devolution of powers from the Eleventh Schedule's 29 subjects is left to state legislatures — it is not compulsory.
• Option (d) — Mandatory: Establishment of a State Election Commission for conducting panchayat elections is obligatory under Article 243K.

Value Addition:
• The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for panchayats; the Twelfth Schedule lists 18 for municipalities.
• State Finance Commissions (mandatory) review financial positions of panchayats every five years.
• The 74th Amendment mirrors the 73rd for urban local bodies — similar mandatory/discretionary distinction applies.

concepts_used: 86th Amendment Act, 2002: Right to Education and Its Three-Dimensional Impact

solution.concept_anchor: Article 21A — age group 6–14 and exclusion of below-6
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who recall the '86th Amendment = RTE' may not remember the precise age bracket, and 0–14 sounds comprehensive and child-welfare oriented.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Article 21A covers children aged 6–14, not 0–14 — children below 6 are covered under Article 45 (DPSP), not as a Fundamental Right.
Eliminate option (c): The age range 0–18 was never part of Article 21A — it overstates the right significantly.
Eliminate option (d): 6–18 is also incorrect; 18 is the voting age, not the RTE boundary.
Confirm option (a): Article 21A specifies children aged 6 to 14 years — this is the precise constitutional text.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The exclusion of children below 6 from Article 21A is a high-frequency UPSC trap. The 86th Amendment simultaneously narrowed Article 45's DPSP to focus on early childhood care for below-6 children, while making education a Fundamental Right only for 6–14. A student who reads 'right to education' and assumes it covers all children from birth will select 0–14 or 0–18.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment (2002) operated on three constitutional provisions simultaneously. It inserted Article 21A, amended Article 45, and added a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A.

• Option (a) — Correct: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education specifically for children between 6 and 14 years of age.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 0–14 is wrong. Children below 6 are covered under the amended Article 45 as a DPSP, not under Article 21A.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 0–18 vastly overstates the scope of Article 21A.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 6–18 is also incorrect; the upper age limit is 14, not 18.

Value Addition:
• The Right to Education Act (2009) was enacted to operationalise Article 21A.
• Article 45 (after 86th Amendment) directs the State to provide early childhood care for children below 6 — it is a DPSP, not a FR.
• Parents/guardians have a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k) to provide educational opportunities to their children aged 6–14.

(d) 6 to 18 years

concepts_used: 91st Amendment Act, 2003: Anti-Defection Law Reforms and Cabinet Size Cap

solution.concept_anchor: 91st Amendment — cabinet size cap and merger threshold

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 raised the threshold for a valid merger under the Tenth Schedule from one-third to two-thirds of the total membership of the legislative party.
statement_analysis.reason: Before the 91st Amendment, one-third of a legislative party could merge with another party without facing disqualification. The 91st Amendment raised this to two-thirds, making it harder to engineer defections through artificial mergers.

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), which caps the total size of the Union Council of Ministers at 10% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: The cap is 15%, not 10%, of the total membership of the House of the People. The minimum strength for state councils of ministers is 12 ministers.

statement_analysis.statement: The 91st Amendment abolished the provision under the Tenth Schedule that allowed a split of one-third members to claim exemption from disqualification.
statement_analysis.reason: Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule, which had allowed a split by one-third members to escape disqualification, was specifically deleted by the 91st Amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and sound complementary, tempting students to accept Statement 2 without verifying the exact percentage.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The merger threshold change from 1/3 to 2/3 is an established feature of the 91st Amendment — correct.
Check Statement 2 precisely: The cap is 15% of Lok Sabha strength, not 10% — Statement 2 is incorrect; eliminate any option that treats it as correct.
Confirm Statement 3: Para 3 (split provision) of the Tenth Schedule was deleted by the 91st Amendment — correct.
With Statements 1 and 3 correct and Statement 2 incorrect, the answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 15% vs. 10% distinction in the cabinet size cap is a precise factual trap. Students who have studied the 91st Amendment in passing may remember the broad idea of a 'percentage cap' without retaining the exact figure. The number 10% appears in other constitutional contexts (quorum in legislatures), making it an effective distractor within the same domain.
solution.final_explanation:
The 91st Amendment (2003) targeted two distinct problems: instability caused by defections through artificial party mergers, and the bloated size of Councils of Ministers.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The merger threshold was raised from 1/3 to 2/3 of legislative party members to qualify as a valid merger under the Tenth Schedule.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 75(1A) caps the Council of Ministers at 15% (not 10%) of Lok Sabha strength. The minimum for state cabinets is 12 ministers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule, which allowed one-third of members to split without disqualification, was deleted — eliminating the 'split' defence entirely.

Value Addition:
• The 15% cap applies separately to the Union Council of Ministers and each State Council of Ministers.
• After the 91st Amendment, the only valid defence against defection disqualification is a merger (2/3rd threshold).
• Voluntary giving up of party membership OR voting against party whip triggers disqualification under Para 2 of the Tenth Schedule.

concepts_used: 99th Amendment Act, 2014 and the NJAC Judgment (2015): Judicial Appointments Controversy

solution.concept_anchor: 99th Amendment NJAC struck down despite state ratification
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students may reason that proper procedural compliance (state ratification) should be an absolute shield — the idea that a validly enacted amendment can still be struck down for Basic Structure violation is counterintuitive.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Supreme Court did not uphold the NJAC — it was struck down; this option is factually false.
Eliminate option (b): State ratification was indeed completed, but the Court held this irrelevant to the Basic Structure question — correct procedure does not immunise against substantive invalidity.
Eliminate option (c): The Law Minister's inclusion was noted as problematic, but the precise holding was about 'primacy of judiciary' in appointments as a Basic Structure element.
Confirm option (d): The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment on the ground that the NJAC compromised judicial independence, which is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The NJAC judgment illustrates that procedural compliance — including state ratification — does not protect a constitutional amendment from Basic Structure challenge. Many students incorrectly assume that if Parliament follows the correct amending procedure (special majority + state ratification), courts cannot invalidate the amendment. This question directly tests that misconception. The correct understanding is that procedural validity and substantive validity are independent requirements.
solution.final_explanation:
The 99th Amendment (2014) replaced the Collegium system with the National Judicial Appointments Commission — a 6-member body comprising the Chief Justice of India, two senior judges, the Union Law Minister, and two 'eminent persons'.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court did not uphold the NJAC — it was unanimously struck down in the 2015 judgment by a 4:1 majority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The amendment had been ratified by more than half the states, satisfying procedural requirements. The Court held that correct procedure cannot save an amendment that violates Basic Structure.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While the Law Minister's inclusion was a concern, the core holding was broader — judicial independence as a Basic Structure element was at stake.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Court held that the NJAC violated judicial independence, which is a component of the Basic Structure, and therefore struck down the amendment.

Value Addition:
• The case is: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015).
• 'Primacy of the judiciary' in judicial appointments was declared a Basic Structure element.
• The Collegium system (evolved through Three Judges Cases) was restored by this judgment.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
The Supreme Court's judgment in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) concerning the 99th Constitutional Amendment is constitutionally significant primarily because it demonstrated that:

(a) The Supreme Court upheld the National Judicial Appointments Commission as consistent with the doctrine of separation of powers
(b) A constitutional amendment ratified by the required number of state legislatures cannot be invalidated by the Supreme Court on any ground
(c) The inclusion of the Union Law Minister in a judicial appointments body violates the basic structure solely on the ground of conflict of interest
(d) Even a constitutionally valid amendment — enacted with proper majority and state ratification — can be struck down if it violates the Basic Structure of the Constitution

concepts_used: 100th Amendment Act, 2015: Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh

solution.concept_anchor: 100th Amendment — enclave exchange numbers and states
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students may recall that the exchange involved Bangladesh and India giving each other different numbers of enclaves, but may swap which side gave more.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Tripura was affected but the amendment covered four states — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura; stating only two affected states is incorrect.
Eliminate option (c): India transferred 111 enclaves TO Bangladesh, not 51. Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India — option (c) reverses the numbers.
Eliminate option (d): The LBA of 1974 was the agreement given effect by this amendment, not an agreement from 2008.
Confirm option (a): India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, and Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India — these numbers are correctly paired.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The enclave exchange numbers (111 by India, 51 by Bangladesh) are a precision trap. Students who recall the exchange but not the direction or the specific numbers will be drawn to option (c), which reverses the figures. The asymmetry — India gave more than it received — is a notable fact that students often get backwards.
solution.final_explanation:
The 100th Amendment (2015) gave constitutional effect to the Land Boundary Agreement of 1974 between India and Bangladesh, under which India and Bangladesh exchanged enclaves — territories of one country surrounded by the other.

• Option (a) — Correct: India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh; Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India. This required amending the First Schedule to reflect the changed territorial descriptions of four states.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Four states were affected — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura — not just two.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This reverses the numbers. India gave 111, Bangladesh gave 51 — not the other way around.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The foundational agreement was signed in 1974, not 2008.

Value Addition:
• The 100th Amendment required state ratification because it altered the First Schedule (territorial descriptions affecting states).
• The four affected states — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura — ratified the amendment.
• This was a rare instance where a constitutional amendment directly altered India's international boundaries.

concepts_used: 101st Amendment Act, 2016: Goods and Services Tax and Fiscal Federalism

solution.concept_anchor: GST Council voting weights and excluded items

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 279A, the GST Council requires decisions to be made by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes cast, where the Central Government has a weightage of one-third of the total votes.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 279A(9) specifies that decisions require a three-fourths majority of weighted votes; the Centre holds 1/3rd and states collectively hold 2/3rd — correctly stated.

statement_analysis.statement: The 101st Amendment completely excluded all petroleum products from the purview of GST, with no provision for their future inclusion even by the GST Council.
statement_analysis.reason: While petroleum products are currently outside GST, Article 279A(5) allows the GST Council to recommend a date from which petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel shall be brought under GST — future inclusion is constitutionally possible.

statement_analysis.statement: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is permanently excluded from GST and cannot be brought under its purview through a GST Council recommendation.
statement_analysis.reason: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded from GST with no provision in the 101st Amendment for its future inclusion through GST Council recommendation — unlike petroleum products, there is no such enabling clause. However, the statement saying 'permanently' and 'cannot be brought' overstates the constitutional position as it conflates the two categories.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because Statement 3 involves a subtle distinction between alcoholic liquor (absolute exclusion) and petroleum products (conditional exclusion), and students may misidentify either as permanently excluded.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The 3/4th majority requirement and Centre's 1/3rd weightage are accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct and cannot be the 'NOT correct' answer.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that there is 'no provision for future inclusion' is false — Article 279A(5) explicitly allows GST Council to bring petroleum products under GST; Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: While alcoholic liquor is excluded with no equivalent enabling clause, 'permanently' and 'cannot' overstate the position — the Constitution does not say 'permanently'; Statement 3 is NOT correct as written.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — option (b) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The distinction between petroleum products (conditionally excluded — GST Council can recommend inclusion) and alcoholic liquor (excluded without a similar enabling clause) is a high-precision area. Students often remember 'petrol and liquor are outside GST' as a single fact without distinguishing the legal mechanism of exclusion. Statement 2 adds the further trap of 'no provision for future inclusion,' which is directly contradicted by Article 279A(5).
solution.final_explanation:
The 101st Amendment (2016) revolutionised India's fiscal federal structure by creating concurrent taxing powers under Article 246A. The GST Council (Article 279A) is the key governance institution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Three-fourths weighted majority is required; Centre has 1/3rd, states collectively 2/3rd.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Petroleum products are excluded from GST currently, but Article 279A(5) explicitly allows the GST Council to recommend a date for their inclusion — 'no provision for future inclusion' is false.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: While alcoholic liquor is excluded without an equivalent inclusion mechanism, describing this as 'permanently cannot be brought' overstates what the Constitution says; and the framing conflates liquor with petroleum products.

Value Addition:
• Five petroleum products currently outside GST: petroleum crude, motor spirit (petrol), high-speed diesel, natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel.
• Tobacco products are within GST but also attract additional Central excise duty.
• The IGST (Integrated GST) applies to inter-state supply of goods and services — managed by the Centre and then apportioned.

concepts_used: 102nd and 105th Amendment Acts: OBC Commission and Reservation in Promotions

solution.concept_anchor: 102nd Amendment NCBC vs 105th Amendment state SEBC power

statement_analysis.statement: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes and introduced Article 342A, which empowers the President to specify Socially and Educationally Backward Classes.
statement_analysis.reason: The 102nd Amendment inserted Article 338B (NCBC) and Article 342A, which established a Presidential power to specify SEBCs — analogous to the President's power for SCs (Article 341) and STs (Article 342).

statement_analysis.statement: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 was enacted to reinforce the 102nd Amendment's position that only the President has the power to identify OBCs, thereby removing any residual state power in this matter.
statement_analysis.reason: The 105th Amendment was enacted to REVERSE the interpretation that removed state power — specifically to restore states' authority to maintain their own SEBC lists, which had been negated by the Supreme Court's interpretation of Article 342A following the 102nd Amendment (Maratha reservation case).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the 102nd and 105th Amendments are connected, and students may assume the 105th Amendment extended or reinforced the 102nd rather than partially reversed its judicial interpretation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 102nd Amendment inserted Articles 338B and 342A — NCBC's constitutional status and Presidential power to specify SEBCs are accurately described; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 105th Amendment was specifically enacted to restore state power to identify OBCs for their own lists — it reversed the SC's Maratha judgment, not reinforced centralization; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The relationship between the 102nd and 105th Amendments is the trap. Students who know both amendments were about OBCs may assume they worked in the same direction — centralising OBC identification. In fact, the 105th Amendment corrected an unintended consequence of the 102nd: after the 102nd Amendment, the Supreme Court held (in the Maratha case) that only the President could notify OBCs, removing state power entirely. The 105th Amendment reversed this to restore state power.
solution.final_explanation:
The 102nd and 105th Amendments together tell a story of legislative response to judicial interpretation gone further than intended.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to NCBC under Article 338B and introduced Article 342A, enabling the President to specify SEBCs for the Central list.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 105th Amendment (2021) was enacted to restore, not reinforce centralization. After the SC interpreted Article 342A as removing state power to identify their own SEBCs, Parliament reversed this through the 105th Amendment — states can maintain their own SEBC lists independently.

Value Addition:
• Pre-102nd Amendment, the NCBC was a statutory body under the NCBC Act, 1993.
• The Maratha reservation case (Indra Sawhney II) was the trigger for the 105th Amendment.
• Article 342A parallels Articles 341 (SCs) and 342 (STs) but is unique in having a state-level parallel list preserved by the 105th Amendment.

concepts_used: Ninth Schedule: Judicial Review Immunity and the I.R. Coelho Judgment

solution.concept_anchor: I.R. Coelho — April 24 1973 cutoff for Ninth Schedule immunity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who recall that Kesavananda Bharati (1973) set the Basic Structure doctrine may not remember the precise date — April 24, 1973 — and may instead assume the cutoff operates from the year 1973 generally.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Laws added before April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute protection — not 'complete immunity regardless of date'; absolute immunity applies only to pre-Kesavananda laws.
Eliminate option (c): The cutoff date is April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda judgment), not January 26, 1950 (Constitution's commencement date).
Eliminate option (d): Laws added after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review for Basic Structure violations — they do not enjoy absolute immunity.
Confirm option (b): The I.R. Coelho judgment established that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be challenged if they violate Basic Structure.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The precise date — April 24, 1973 — is the critical detail. This is the date the Kesavananda Bharati judgment was pronounced, and I.R. Coelho used this as the cutoff for Ninth Schedule immunity. Students who know the year (1973) but not the date may select option (a), which implies a blanket immunity without a date-specific distinction. The date also risks confusion with January 26, 1950 (Constitution's commencement) which appears in option (c) as a plausible-sounding alternative.
solution.final_explanation:
The I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) judgment by a 9-judge bench fundamentally changed the understanding of Ninth Schedule immunity.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Absolute immunity is not the universal rule; it applies only to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
• Option (b) — Correct: Laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the Kesavananda judgment date) are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: January 26, 1950 is the Constitution's commencement date, not the I.R. Coelho cutoff.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Reverses the rule — pre-1973 laws are protected; post-1973 laws are reviewable.

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule grew from 13 laws (1951) to 284 laws, with many added after 1973.
• April 24, 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati pronouncement — a key constitutional calendar date.
• The I.R. Coelho ruling effectively subjects post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to Part III scrutiny filtered through the Basic Structure test.

(b) Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution
(c) The cutoff date for Ninth Schedule immunity is January 26, 1950 — laws placed in the Schedule after the Constitution came into force are reviewable

concepts_used: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Limits on Parliament's Amending Power

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — original vs expanded Article 31C

statement_analysis.statement: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the expanded version of Article 31C inserted by the 42nd Amendment, which had given all Directive Principles primacy over all Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The 42nd Amendment had expanded Article 31C to protect laws implementing any DPSP from Fundamental Rights challenges. Minerva Mills struck this down while retaining the original Article 31C (protecting laws under Articles 39(b) and 39(c) only).

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills also struck down the original Article 31C inserted by the 25th Amendment, which protected laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) of the Directive Principles.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Article 31C — protecting laws aimed at achieving Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — was specifically upheld in Minerva Mills; only the expanded version covering all DPSPs was struck down.

statement_analysis.statement: The Minerva Mills judgment declared that the harmonious balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself an element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Court held in Minerva Mills that the balance between Parts III and IV of the Constitution — between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles — is a core element of the Basic Structure that Parliament cannot destroy.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is tempting because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and may lead students to carelessly accept Statement 2 without recalling the specific distinction between the original and expanded Article 31C.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The expanded Article 31C (all DPSPs over all FRs) was struck down in Minerva Mills — correct.
Test Statement 2: The original Article 31C (39(b) and 39(c) only) was UPHELD, not struck down — Statement 2 is incorrect; eliminate options treating it as correct.
Confirm Statement 3: Harmony between FR and DPSP as a Basic Structure element was explicitly declared in Minerva Mills — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The original vs. expanded Article 31C is the precision trap. Both versions of Article 31C are real; only the expanded version was struck down. A student who remembers 'Minerva Mills struck down Article 31C' without distinguishing original from expanded will incorrectly accept Statement 2 as correct, selecting option (d). The two-tier nature of Article 31C's history is a favourite UPSC testing dimension.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills (1980) is the third pillar of the amendment-judicial review trilogy, and its most important contribution was clarifying the limits of parliamentary amendment power and the relationship between Parts III and IV.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The expanded Article 31C (from 42nd Amendment), which gave all DPSPs supremacy over all Fundamental Rights, was struck down as destroying the constitutional balance.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The original Article 31C from the 25th Amendment — protecting laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — was specifically upheld, not struck down.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Court declared that harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a Basic Structure element — Parliament cannot tilt the balance entirely in favour of either.

Value Addition:
• Articles 39(b) and 39(c) concern equitable distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
• Minerva Mills also held that limited amending power is a Basic Structure element — Parliament cannot grant itself unlimited amending power.
• The judgment restored the balance that the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment had disrupted.

solution.concept_anchor: 104th Amendment — SC/ST reservation extended, Anglo-Indian seats abolished
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may correctly recall that the 104th Amendment abolished Anglo-Indian nominated seats and assume the Reason about SC/ST reservation being a separate provision is somehow incorrect.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 104th Amendment (2019) abolished nominated Anglo-Indian seats in Lok Sabha (Article 331) and state assemblies (Article 333).

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The 104th Amendment also extended the reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and state assemblies for a further 10 years (2020 to 2030) by amending Article 334.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The abolition of Anglo-Indian seats and the extension of SC/ST reservation are two independent actions in the same amendment — one did not cause or logically explain the other.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may conflate the two changes made by the 104th Amendment — abolition of Anglo-Indian seats and extension of SC/ST reservation — into a single narrative of 'minority representation changes.' The trap is that R (extension of SC/ST reservation) is factually true but is a separate action with no causal connection to A (abolition of Anglo-Indian seats). Both happened in the same amendment but for entirely independent policy reasons.
solution.final_explanation:
The 104th Amendment (2019) made two structurally distinct changes to the Constitution. These changes were both part of the same amending act but arose from completely different policy rationales.

Assertion analysis: Articles 331 and 333, which provided for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to Parliament and state assemblies, were abolished — Assertion is correct.

Reason analysis: Article 334 was amended to extend reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and state assemblies for another 10 years (until 2030) — Reason is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The abolition of Anglo-Indian seats was driven by the community's declining demographic presence; the extension of SC/ST reservation reflects continued socio-economic need. These are independent policy choices — not causally linked.

Value Addition:
• Anglo-Indian nominated seats had been periodically extended since the Constitution came into force — the 104th Amendment ended this practice.
• Article 334 originally set 10 years for SC/ST reservation; it has been extended multiple times through amendment.
• SC/ST reservation in legislatures is for seats, not for nomination — they contest general elections in reserved constituencies.

solution.concept_anchor: Golak Nath–24th Amendment–Kesavananda–42nd Amendment–Minerva Mills sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know the broad sequence (Golak Nath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills) may forget that the 24th Amendment came between Golak Nath and Kesavananda, and place the 42nd Amendment incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was decided in 1967 — it comes first in the sequence.
The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's response to Golak Nath — it comes after Golak Nath but before Kesavananda.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) responded to the 24th Amendment — it comes next, establishing Basic Structure.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) was Parliament's response to Kesavananda — it comes after; then Minerva Mills (1980) responded to the 42nd Amendment. Correct sequence: Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in the interleaved sequence of judicial decisions and constitutional amendments. Students who study judicial cases and constitutional amendments in separate silos know the sequence within each category but may fail to correctly interleave them. The most common error is placing the 42nd Amendment before Kesavananda (wrong — the 42nd Amendment was a response to Kesavananda) or placing the 24th Amendment after Kesavananda.
solution.final_explanation:
The Golak Nath–Kesavananda–Minerva Mills trilogy is not purely judicial — it is a back-and-forth between Parliament (through amendments) and the judiciary (through judgments). Understanding the interleaved sequence is essential.

Correct sequence:
1. Golak Nath (1967): FR cannot be amended at all.
2. 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament's response — FR can be amended; Article 13 and 368 modified.
3. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): FR can be amended but Basic Structure cannot be destroyed.
4. 42nd Amendment (1976): Parliament's response — attempted to grant itself unlimited amending power (struck down later).
5. Minerva Mills (1980): Supreme Court's response — struck down the 42nd Amendment's Clauses 4 and 5; limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure element.

Why other options fail: Options (a), (b), and (d) incorrectly interleave the judicial and legislative responses.

Value Addition:
• Each amendment was a direct parliamentary retaliation against the preceding judicial decision.
• The 25th Amendment (1971) was also part of this period — it inserted Article 31C.
• Prospective overruling was applied for the first time in Indian law in Golak Nath.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 368 — what falls outside its procedure

statement_analysis.statement: Admission of new states into the Union under Article 2 is amendable by simple majority and does not fall within the ambit of Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit new states by law — this is a legislative power exercisable by simple majority and is explicitly outside the Article 368 amendment procedure.

statement_analysis.statement: Change in the name or boundaries of existing states under Article 3 requires a special majority under Article 368 and state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 changes (alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of states) require only a simple majority in Parliament — they are outside Article 368 and do not require state ratification, though affected state legislatures are consulted.

statement_analysis.statement: Abolition of the Legislative Council of a state under Article 169 is effected by Parliament by simple majority after the state assembly passes a resolution — it operates outside Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 169 provides for abolition or creation of state legislative councils — Parliament passes the law by simple majority after the state assembly resolves, and Article 369 clarifies this is not an amendment under Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: The quorum requirements for Parliament under Article 100 can be altered by Parliament through the Article 368 special majority procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100 (quorum) is amendable by simple majority — it is among the provisions that fall outside Article 368's scope and do not require the special majority or state ratification procedure.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is tempting because students may correctly identify Articles 2 and 169 as outside Article 368 but may believe Article 3 requires Article 368's procedure given its federal implications.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 2 (admission of states) is by ordinary legislation, outside Article 368.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 3 changes also require only simple majority; they are outside Article 368 despite their territorial significance.
Statement 3 is correct — Article 169 operates by ordinary parliamentary law after state assembly resolution; outside Article 368.
Statement 4 is incorrect — Article 100 (quorum) is amendable by simple majority, not special majority under Article 368. Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here affects both Statement 2 and Statement 4. Students assume that provisions with federal or structural significance (like changing state boundaries under Article 3, or quorum requirements under Article 100) must require the more demanding Article 368 procedure. In reality, these are among the expressly simple-majority provisions that operate entirely outside Article 368 — a fact that contradicts intuitive reasoning about constitutional gravity.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 governs only a subset of constitutional amendments — not all changes to the Constitution require its procedure. Many provisions are amendable by ordinary legislative majority.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 2 (admission of states) requires only a parliamentary law by simple majority.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 3 changes (state boundaries/names) require only simple majority — the state legislature is consulted but need not concur, and Article 368 does not apply.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 169 operates outside Article 368; it requires a state assembly resolution followed by a simple-majority parliamentary law.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 100 (quorum = 1/10th of total membership) can be altered by Parliament without invoking Article 368's special majority requirement.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is 'Only two'.

Value Addition:
• Other simple-majority provisions outside Article 368: creation of new All India Services (Article 312), salaries of Parliament members.
• State ratification is required for ~8–10 specific categories — not for the majority of constitutional changes.
• Consultation with state legislature under Article 3 is not consent — Parliament can override state objections.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd vs 44th Amendment features — precise attribution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know the 42nd Amendment added Fundamental Duties and the 44th Amendment restored the 5-year term may correctly place A and B but then swap C and D.
elimination_logic: A (Words 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' added to Preamble) → 42nd Amendment (1976); matches List II item 2.
B (Restoration of 5-year term for Lok Sabha) → 44th Amendment (1978); matches List II item 4.
C (Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights) → 44th Amendment (1978); matches List II item 3.
D (Addition of Fundamental Duties under Part IVA) → 42nd Amendment (1976); matches List II item 1. Correct: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap operates between the 42nd and 44th Amendments, which are closely related in the Emergency and post-Emergency period. Students know both are important but may attribute features of one to the other. Specifically, the Right to Property deletion (44th Amendment) and the addition of Fundamental Duties (42nd Amendment) are commonly confused in attribution.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd and 44th Amendments bracket the Emergency period — the former enacted during Emergency (1976), the latter as a corrective after (1978).

• A (Words 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' in Preamble) → 42nd Amendment (1976). These words reflected the ideological framing of the Emergency era.
• B (Restoration of 5-year Lok Sabha term) → 44th Amendment (1978). The 42nd had extended terms to 6 years; the 44th reversed this.
• C (Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights) → 44th Amendment (1978). Property became a legal right under Article 300A.
• D (Fundamental Duties added, Part IVA, Article 51A) → 42nd Amendment (1976). Originally 10 duties were added.

Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

Value Addition:
• The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Amendment (2002): duty to provide education opportunities to children.
• The 42nd Amendment also extended Lok Sabha and state assembly terms from 5 to 6 years (reversed by 44th).
• Articles 20 and 21 were declared non-suspendable even during Emergency by the 44th Amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: 91st Amendment — cabinet size 15% of Lok Sabha strength
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 10% appears in constitutional contexts (quorum under Article 100) and students who recall 'a percentage of Lok Sabha' may default to 10 without verifying the precise figure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): 20% of Lok Sabha strength (543 seats) would mean 108 ministers — this would be an extremely large cabinet and is not the constitutional provision.
Eliminate option (b): 10% is the quorum requirement under Article 100, not the cabinet size cap — a different constitutional number.
Eliminate option (c): 25% would allow 135+ ministers and is not the cap prescribed in Article 75(1A).
Confirm option (d): Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 15% figure is a precision trap. Constitutional percentages cluster in a student's memory — 10% (quorum), 1/3 and 2/3 (defection), 3/4 (GST Council). The 15% cabinet cap is a specific statutory ceiling that is easy to confuse with 10% or 20% without precise recall. The minimum of 12 for state councils is an additional detail that further tests precision.
solution.final_explanation:
The 91st Amendment (2003) introduced a constitutional ceiling on the size of the Council of Ministers to prevent the practice of distributing cabinet berths for political management rather than governance efficiency.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 20% of Lok Sabha strength is not the constitutional cap.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 10% is the quorum requirement in Parliament under Article 100 — a different constitutional provision.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 25% is not the prescribed limit.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 75(1A) caps the Union Council of Ministers at 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha. For state councils, the minimum is 12 ministers and the ceiling is 15% of the state assembly's strength.

Value Addition:
• At Lok Sabha strength of 543, the maximum Union cabinet size is approximately 81 ministers.
• The 15% cap applies separately to each state — states cannot pool limits.
• The 91st Amendment simultaneously raised the merger threshold in the Tenth Schedule from 1/3 to 2/3.

solution.concept_anchor: Basic Structure — procedurally valid amendment still reviewable
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the scenario describes a constitutionally perfect procedure — special majority and state ratification — which students may assume renders the amendment beyond challenge.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Procedural correctness (special majority + state ratification) does not immunise a constitutional amendment from Basic Structure challenge — the NJAC case is direct precedent for this.

Eliminate option (c): Article 32 petitions relate to enforcement of Fundamental Rights, not to challenge of constitutional amendments — the jurisdictional basis would be the Court's power of judicial review of constitutional amendments.
Eliminate option (d): Courts can review constitutional amendments even if enacted with correct procedure — the Basic Structure doctrine operates as a substantive limit, not a procedural one.

Confirm option (b): The amendment can be challenged on the ground that it damages a Basic Structure element, regardless of procedural compliance — the principle established across Kesavananda, Minerva Mills, and the NJAC judgment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question tests the misconception that procedural compliance with Article 368 provides an absolute shield. The NJAC judgment directly established that even an amendment ratified by more than half the states can be struck down if it violates the Basic Structure. A student who conflates 'constitutionally enacted' with 'judicially unreviewable' will select option (a). The scenario is designed to present the most procedurally sound amendment possible to maximise this trap's effectiveness.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario presents a constitutionally enacted amendment — special majority and state ratification obtained — and tests whether procedural validity insulates it from judicial review.

Applicable principle: The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; reinforced in Minerva Mills, 1980 and NJAC, 2015) holds that Parliament's amending power has substantive limits — it cannot destroy the Constitution's basic features, regardless of how the amendment was enacted.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The NJAC judgment (2015) is direct precedent that state ratification + special majority is not an absolute shield. The Court struck down the 99th Amendment despite valid enactment.
• Option (b) — Correct: The affected stakeholder can challenge the amendment before the Supreme Court on the ground that it violates a Basic Structure element — substantive review is independent of procedural compliance.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 32 is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights against State action, not for challenging constitutional amendments — the jurisdictional basis would be the Court's inherent power of judicial review over constitutional validity.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: This restates the erroneous assumption that the scenario is designed to challenge.

Value Addition:
• The 99th Amendment was ratified by more than half the states yet was struck down — the clearest modern illustration of this principle.
• Basic Structure review is a substantive test, not a procedural one.
• Limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure element (Minerva Mills) — creating a self-referential protection.
